content.thinking:
I'm planning out the chopper motorbike design in an Overwatch-inspired style—polished bold shapes, dark gunmetal with an orange accent, sized around 2.3m long and 1.1m to the handlebars, oriented facing forward along Z with wheels on the X axis and the floor at y=0. Now I'm setting up the builder imports to start constructing it.

Working out wheel geometry using torus shapes rotated to align their axis along X, with different radii for a fatter rear tire versus a leaner front one, making sure both sit flush on the ground. I'm also defining a cylinder helper rotated to lie along the X axis for rods and connecting parts, then starting to lay out the rear wheel's position in the overall frame.

Now I'm placing the front wheel further forward to create a raked chopper fork and a roughly 2.7 meter total length, then positioning the V-twin engine at the bike's center with angled cylinder heads and cooling fins. I'm sketching out the hardtail frame tubes connecting the neck, seat post, down tube, engine cradle, and rear axle stays to tie the whole structure together.

Working out the fork geometry with its 35-38 degree rake, calculating the triple tree position above the headstock and the lower fork tube endpoints that reach down to the front axle.

For the fork sliders, I'm planning a thin chrome stanchion for the upper section transitioning to a thicker dark lower tube near the axle. Now I'm sketching the ape-hanger handlebars rising up from the headstock with a curved sweep outward and upward from the grips.

Next I'm placing a round headlamp just in front of the fork, positioning it slightly forward of the headstock with a glow lens facing outward.

For the tank, I'm lofting a teardrop shape along the top of the frame, running from the headstock back toward the seat area, with a custom paint gradient giving it a dark base and an orange accent stripe for contrast.

For the seat, I'm extruding a slim tucked outline in the side profile, giving it a thin angular shape that tapers from front to back.

For the fenders, I'm sweeping a thin arc path over the rear wheel to form a curved tube-like shape, positioning it around the axle radius.

Ending the arc at rear horizontal gives a nice short bobber fender, with a 0.06 gap over the tire and a narrow box-section width of about 0.14. I'm now deciding on colors, leaning toward a dark gunmetal fender body with a single accent edge in an Overwatch-style palette.

For the overall palette I'm settling on dark graphite, light off-white, mid steel-gray, a single orange accent, chrome, and black rubber, with headlight glow warm-white and taillight glow orange-red. For the front fender, I'm sizing it to arc over the front wheel with a radius of 0.4 and need to make sure the fork tubes clear the fender's width so they visually sit outside it.

Now I'm working out the wheel geometry: tire half-width, axle and fork positions, and a chunkier rear tire with a wider fender, then figuring out how to build the rims as cast six-spoke stars using a hub disc and rod-shaped spokes positioned radially plus a surrounding rim torus.

For the rear rim I'll use solid disc "mag" covers with a hub radius and an orange accent ring made from a torus decal, built from simple 12-sided cylinders rather than spokes. Now I'm moving on to the engine, starting with the crankcase.

For the crankcase I'm placing a dark box slung low in the frame cradle, then adding two angled cylinder barrels splayed forward and backward from the crank position to mimic a V-twin layout, with cooling fins made from stacked thin discs along each barrel.

I'm also adding chrome cylinder heads above the barrels and routing curved exhaust pipes down from the front head, sweeping back along the frame toward the rear using a smooth curve through several guide points.

I'm mirroring a second exhaust pipe on the other side from the front cylinder, keeping both as simple drag pipes with chrome bodies and darker flared end caps. For the rear cylinder I'm placing a round air filter and a chrome intake carb body, adjusting its position so it doesn't overlap the rear cylinder's barrel location.

Now I'm working through vertical placement math for the cylinders, tank, and heads — tweaking tilt angle and lengths so the tank bottom clears the cylinder head tops without too much overlap, settling on a tank center height and the cylinder's tilted top edge position.

Overall height lands around 1.3 with handlebars, seat around 0.8, tank top near 1.10. I accept the frame top tube will pass hidden inside the tank visually, which is fine since it's not visible anyway. Now I'm adding the primary drive side cover as a small lathed disc with an orange ring, and starting on the belt sweep geometry.

Then I'll add the belt rod running down to the rear axle with a thin rubber box and a rear sprocket disc, plus forward foot control pegs as small cylindrical rods with mounting hardware. I'm skipping a kickstand since the bike sits upright on both wheels as a static asset, and there's no rear shock since it's a hardtail. For the tail end, I'm placing a glowing tail lamp on the fender at a rearward angle, working out its position along the fender's curve.

Adding handlebar grips, small lever rods, round mirrors on stalks, and a glowing speedo gauge cylinder on top of the headlight, plus risers.

For the tank design, I'm skipping decal textures and instead painting an orange stripe directly onto the tank surface, trying to position it using the tank's sweep-based coordinate system at a specific point along its length and angle.

I need to figure out the decal's reading orientation on each side — working out that for a viewer on the +X side facing -X, "right" points toward -Z, meaning the chevron orientation differs between sides and I'll need to mirror the decal for the opposite face so the symbol reads correctly from both sides.

Now I'm sketching the decal texture itself: an angular orange/white stripe pattern with transparent cutouts, sized small on the surface, plus a similar bold geometric slash decal for an "Overwatch" style marking. I'm also setting up a reusable paint helper for giving painted metal a subtle top-lit gradient look, and planning an orange panel stripe along the tank body using a position-based mask.

Still defining panel stripes...

I'm estimating total part count across wheels, spokes, fins, and bolts to stay well under a reasonable budget, and sketching a bolt helper using small spheres. For the tank body I'm laying out loft stations front-to-back with varying width/height ellipses to shape the hull profile.

I'm checking that the tank, seat, and frame tubes sit together reasonably -- seat height clears the tank rear, and the top frame tube needs to run from near the tank down toward the rear to support the seat.

Now I'm plotting the main spine: the down tube from the neck sweeping down into the cradle, then up into the seat tube, using a thin catmull rod. For the rear triangle, I'm placing paired stays running from the cradle and seat area out to the rear axle position, checking their x-offset clears the rear tire's torus radius.

For the front end, I'm computing the head tube orientation and length, then working out the fork geometry from the headstock down to the front axle -- accounting for a slight forward offset to get the right rake angle, landing around 38 degrees based on the vector between the fork top and axle points.

Now I'm checking wheelbase and overall bike length for proportions, then sketching out the triple tree plates as thin boxes aligned along the fork's axis direction so they sit correctly between the fork tubes.

I'm building the fork slider assembly with a chrome upper stanchion and darker lower slider piece transitioning partway down toward the axle, then placing the headlight by figuring out where the fork's position lands at a given height so it sits centered in front of the bike.

Adding the headlight shell with a gunmetal bucket and orange accent ring, then positioning a small speedometer cylinder near the handlebar clamp angled toward the rider.

Now I'm sketching the handlebar sweep geometry, mirroring the curve for both sides and building a chrome tube path from the clamp up to the grips.

I'm placing the rubber grips with orange end caps, adding thin lever rods angled toward the grip area, and figuring out mirror stalk placement and height on each side.

Skipping bar-mounted mirrors in favor of simple orange bar-end caps, and now positioning forward control pegs with rubber grips, rear pegs, and the support rods connecting them to the frame. I'm placing the oil tank cylinder under the seat and a battery box on the opposite side with a dark finish and decal, then starting on the exhaust pipe sweep with a flared end and a heat shield.

Mapping out exhaust pipe coordinates...

Skipping the second pipe idea for an air filter instead, and checking that the pipes clear the crankcase sides at both heights—looks fine. For the pipe tips, I'll just use rounded end caps rather than a flared cone.

Now moving to engine details: I'm laying out cylinder fins as a series of rings along the cylinder axis with a solid barrel core, plus smaller orange rocker covers and chrome pushrod tubes beside each cylinder. For the carb/air cleaner, I'm placing a chrome cylinder outside the V-gap between the two cylinder banks, checking the geometry so it doesn't collide with the cylinders themselves.

For the primary cover and gas cap, I'm positioning chrome cylinders at the appropriate mounting points with orange accent rings (using torus shapes rotated so their axis aligns correctly), plus a bolt ring pattern. I'm also adding decorative touches like a tank stripe, side decals, and rubber knee pads approximated with scaled spheres near the tank sides.

For the seat, I'm painting a dark leather base with subtle grey stitching lines running across the surface where the normal points upward. For the wheels, I'm placing chrome hubs with orange cap discs, a front brake disc with an orange caliper box positioned against the fork slider, and a rear sprocket disc with a belt rod connecting to the primary cover position.

Now I'm working out the belt geometry between the primary and rear sprocket, running two rod sections top and bottom with small radius for a rubber-belt look, and checking that the belt's path at x=0.13 doesn't collide with the rear fender arc or tire width.

For the rear wheel discs, I'm sizing side covers around r 0.17 with the tire's inner radius at 0.18, adding an orange rim torus, then painting a procedural spoke pattern on the disc using polar coordinates—five wedge spokes with a chrome hub center and orange rim edge.

I want the same treatment mirrored on both sides of the rear disc, then switch to real rod-based spokes for the front wheel instead. For the tire tread, I'm using the torus UV coordinates to paint groove and chevron patterns along the rolling direction, plus a sidewall stripe band positioned around the tube's midline.

For the rear torus I'll use 8 radial by 28 tubular segments, and 6x28 for the front; since the paint is baked into a texture mapped by UV, coarse segment counts should still look fine with linear interpolation.

I'm checking three.js geometries for their built-in UV attributes, which should work for the painted surfaces since they sample color using UV coordinates directly. For paint resolution, I'll keep the default texture size rather than bumping to 2048 or 4096, since that gets heavy fast, and I'm trying to recall the right builder setup—something like initializing a builder with a name parameter and returning its root object.

I'm working out the correct imports: pulling createBuilder from the builder module, and arc/catmull/polyline helpers from the path module, with arc taking center, start point, axis, and angle in degrees. I need to watch for unused imports causing typecheck errors, and keep point/vector types as plain number arrays throughout.

For the decal textures, I'm sketching SVG artwork—a tank marking with an orange parallelogram, a white bar, and some stenciled text like "VX-9" with a dark outline, plus a separate plate SVG with rectangle and text elements, and figuring out the decal placement and sizing options.

Writing builder setup code...

Adding bolt helper functions...

Now I'm defining the color palette - graphite, white, steel, orange accents, chrome, rubber, and seat tones for the materials.

I'm setting up a shading function that mixes base and lit colors based on surface normal, then writing the loop to generate engine cylinders from control points...

Adding fin geometry details...

Still laying out engine parts...

Computing spoke geometry...

Still placing wheel geometry... now adding a disc brake cylinder near the front wheel and sizing the rear tire torus with matching brake discs on both sides.

Still writing paint pattern logic...

Now thinking through the fenders, sweeping arcs with a radius function to shape the cross-section, setting orientation so the thin dimension sits radially along the wheel arc.

I'm deciding on an overall color scheme: white/steel body panels with graphite accents, chrome frame and engine, and bold orange stripe accents down the center of the fenders and tank for a sporty look, with the paint function blending between stripe, graphite edge, and shaded body color based on normal direction.

Now I'm working out the geometry for the front fender arc, positioning it over the front tire with appropriate radius and angular sweep so it wraps correctly above the wheel, while also accounting for the fork tubes on either side.

For the taillight, I'm calculating its position along the rear fender using a trigonometric offset from the mounting angle, then figuring out the rotation needed to align the glowing lamp box flush against the fender's slope.

Adding plate orientation and mount details...

Now checking bolts for tank, fork tree, and covers, plus a few finishing touches like the front master cylinder and a control cable sweeping from lever to headlight.

Adding fender support struts connecting the rear axle up to the fender at an angle, while skipping extra details like brake lines, kickstand, and chain since the belt drive already covers that function.

Still writing part types and helper functions...

Now I'm laying out the fork assembly pieces—stanchions, sliders with the orange band, axle caps—and positioning the front axles and frame pieces like the head tube relative to the fork's center point.

Still planning the frame geometry...

Now I'm adding footpegs with rubber-sleeved mounts, rear pegs, and considering oil tank and battery placement, then planning a tank decal texture using SVG.

Writing SVG code...

For mirroring on the opposite side, I'm deciding to skip flipping the text so it stays readable from both viewing angles.

I'm placing the decal on the tank surface using azimuth and elevation coordinates, then setting the loft stations and side count for the tank geometry.

I'm sketching out the headlight shell and fender paint colors, then turning to the file metadata (name, description, style, commit hash) and checking that the arc and catmull path functions handle the point arrays correctly. I'm also verifying the floor contact math so the rear and front tires sit exactly at y=0 given their torus radii.

I confirm the torus tubular and radial segment counts align so the lowest vertex actually touches the ground rather than floating slightly above it, and double-check the oil pan's bottom height matches. Now I'm writing the tread paint function...

Still placing headlamp brackets and speedometer housing...
